strengths: MaskSub offers a simple, technically coherent way to combine supervised learning with heavy masking: the masked view learns from detached predictions of the full view using shared parameters. It adds no inference cost or model parameters and integrates readily with existing training recipes.

The core ImageNet results are convincing. Table 1 reports improvements across ViT-S/B/L/H and both training lengths. The repeated experiments strengthen this evidence: Table A.13 reports ViT-B improving from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02 at 400 epochs.

The paper meaningfully addresses additional training cost. Table 8 shows ViT-B reaching 84.1% in 25 GPU-days versus 83.7% for longer baseline training in 26 GPU-days. Table 9 also demonstrates a favorable accuracy–cost tradeoff against CoSub and other augmentation methods.

Evaluation extends substantially beyond ImageNet classification, covering pretrained-model finetuning, ResNet and Swin, semantic segmentation, detection, and robustness. For example, Table 10 shows consistent ADE20K improvements, while Table A.4 reports ViT-L ImageNet-A accuracy increasing from 45.3% to 51.1%. These results support practical value for computer vision.

The appendix provides useful ablations on distillation, masking ratios, loss weights, and alternative drop regularizations, alongside repeated runs and detailed training recipes. Algorithm 1 and the supplied code link further support reproducibility. This empirical support makes the case for acceptance stronger than the reservations below.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited relative to existing asymmetric consistency training and self-distillation. In particular, Eq. (3), with its detached target, has the same student gradient as KL consistency loss. Section 2's distinction between MaskSub's distillation loss and UDA's consistency loss therefore does not establish a fundamentally different objective. The strongest contribution is the effective supervised training recipe and its validation.

The automatic difficulty-control explanation exceeds the evidence. Figure 2 supports an aggregate gradient trend, but the method does not explicitly restrict masked supervision to correctly predicted examples, as the text suggests; confidently incorrect teacher predictions can also provide strong supervision. Moreover, stop-gradient detaches the target while both branches still update shared parameters. These qualifications affect the mechanistic interpretation, rather than the validity of the implemented objective.

Benefits are not universal. Applying MaskSub during finetuning reduces ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy from 91.89% to 89.55% with the same MaskSub-pretrained backbone (Table A.10). Section 4.2 also acknowledges that CLIP's best-checkpoint performance is unchanged. Small gains such as BEiTv2's 0.1 percentage point lack reported variability, so the broad claims of consistent improvement need qualification.

Some comparisons provide weaker evidence than the main ViT experiments. Table 6 mixes training recipes for several self-distillation methods, although the RSB reruns for two methods are useful; the heterogeneous comparisons do not establish general incompatibility with strong recipes. Efficiency also depends on architecture: ResNet and Swin require approximately twice the training computation, and equivalent-budget comparisons are not provided for every extension.

Minor presentation issues include the duplicated CIFAR100 headings in Table 7 and Table 12's ambiguous description of masking vision and language, whereas Appendix B specifies image-only masking. These are readily correctable and do not determine the recommendation.
